props.command: If an outcome has probability 0.665 and I sample it 1000 times, why doesn't it show up 665 times?
output: recorded main.py output · reconstructed Claude UI

beats.narration_text: Think of it like a weighted die. Outcome two comes up sixty-six point five percent of the time. Roll it a thousand times, and you'd expect it to land near six hundred sixty-five. But 'expect' doesn't mean 'guaranteed'.

show.event: Artifact card, three staggered lines: 'Outcome 2 comes up 66.5% of the time.' / '1,000 rolls → expect near 665.' / 'Expected doesn't mean guaranteed.'

artifactLines: Outcome 2 comes up 66.5% of the time.

beats.narration_text: Here's the actual code. It sets the odds, rolls a thousand times, and counts what happens. Nothing in the code forces the final count to match the odds exactly — each roll is independent.

props.title: main.py · course reference, unmodified · lines 9–24

beats.narration_text: Three outcomes: zero, one, and two. Their odds are nine percent, twenty-four and a half percent, and sixty-six and a half percent. Multiply each by a thousand rolls, and that's what you'd expect on average: about ninety, about two hundred forty-five, about six hundred sixty-five.

shot.artifact: ExecutedData bars from recorded main.py stdout

beats.narration_text: Here's what this run actually got: one hundred two, two hundred sixty-eight, and six hundred thirty. Outcome two came up thirty-five fewer times than expected. Think about flipping a coin ten times — you expect five heads, but getting six or four wouldn't surprise anyone. This is the same idea at a bigger scale — though, as we'll see next, this gap is bigger than a four or a six.

props.title: Expected vs. observed count
props.note: Outcome 0: expected 90.03, observed 102 · recorded output · source: lessons/01-randomness-and-first-prompts/code/main.py -> counts {"1": 268, "2": 630, "0": 102}

beats.narration_text: Is thirty-five a lot? At this scale, this count normally wanders by about fifteen in either direction, just from chance. Coming up thirty-five short is on the unusual side — it would happen by chance roughly once in every hundred tries. Unusual, but not impossible.

props.title: Is a 35-count gap a lot?
props.note: computed from output · source: lessons/01-randomness-and-first-prompts/code/main.py -> counts {"1": 268, "2": 630, "0": 102} · n = 1,000, p = 0.665

beats.narration_text: Here's the limit. This code always uses the same starting point, called a seed, so it prints six thirty every single time you rerun it. Getting the same result twice doesn't prove it's fair — it just proves it's repeatable.

shot.artifact: main.py lines 19–22 and 26–28 verbatim; two reruns produced byte-identical stdout (FACTCHECK.md C9)

props.title: main.py · course reference · lines 19–22 and 26–28

beats.narration_text: One run is one data point. It can't tell bad luck apart from a biased die. Telling those apart takes many rolls with different starting points — and this assignment only ran one.

shot.artifact: Boundary card: what the single seeded run does not establish (FACTCHECK.md C10)

show.event: Three plain lines: one data point · can't separate bad luck from bias · needs many seeds

props.heading: What This Does Not Show
props.body: One run is one data point. It can't tell bad luck apart from a biased die. Telling those apart takes many rolls with different starting points — and this assignment only ran one.

beats.narration_text: The takeaway: expected and observed counts can differ just by chance, even when the odds are completely correct. This particular gap is on the larger side, but it isn't proof that anything is broken.

artifactLines: Gap ≈ 2.4 × typical wander: unusual, possible by chance.
